title: When the Search for the Right Answer Isn’t a Search
author: Admired Leadership
summary: A short argument that teams routinely talk past one another about what “the right answer” even means. The piece distinguishes two operating definitions: the objectively most accurate or effective conclusion, and the conclusion most endorsed by the room’s most powerful, senior or credentialed people. Those holding the second definition quietly withhold counter-arguments and competing evidence, not out of laziness but out of a desire to support others — which is especially damaging when the silent party is the subject-matter expert on the decision at hand. The remedy offered is definitional and procedural: leaders should state explicitly what standard of rightness the group is using, insist every participant voice a candid view, and treat everyone as peers so that deference to status has nothing to grip. The closing move is deliberately provocative, recasting empathy as a liability in group decision-making because it redirects attention from objective truths toward how colleagues feel about the issue.
points: Two incompatible definitions of ‘the right answer’ — most accurate versus most endorsed — can coexist at one table without anyone noticing, which is what makes the problem subversive rather than obvious.
The damage scales with expertise: when the person deferring is the subject-matter expert, their withheld candour distorts the conclusion most.
The proposed fix is to make the standard explicit up front and to flatten status in the room, so that agreeing with others stops being a substitute for reasoning.
The author argues the diagnostic is in the questions asked — questions about objective truths versus questions about how others feel about the issue.
A deliberately counterintuitive closing claim: in collective decision-making, empathy can be a killer.
quotes: What constitutes the so-called right answer in the minds of leaders and team members varies more than we generally believe.
The logical presumption is that the right answer is always the most effective or most accurate conclusion.
In other words, the right answer is the one the most powerful or wise or experienced colleagues say it is. Objective reality takes a backseat to how others subjectively view the answer.
Their goal is not to reach the objectively best conclusion, but rather to prop up whatever answer others most believe in.
Good leaders make sure everyone understands what is meant by the right answer. They insist that everyone at the table offer their candid views about the best choice or path forward.
Without everyone committed to landing on the objectively right answer, teams make poor decisions, sometimes with devastating consequences.
Those questions are always about objective truths and not about how we think others feel about the issue. When it comes to making decisions together, empathy can be a killer.
